messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Priya is a 23-year-old UX designer who came to treatment months after a car accident in which she had been driving and seriously injured a pedestrian. She describes the moment with a painful precision that has not softened with time: she had been turning through a busy downtown intersection after work, tired, thinking about a deadline, when she saw movement too late and felt the sickening impact. She remembers the pedestrian on the pavement, the unnatural stillness and then the sudden crowd, someone shouting for an ambulance, and the glimpse of a young woman kneeling beside him. What has stayed with her most is not only that she was the driver, but the ordinary setting of it — the office district, the end-of-day traffic, people in work clothes crossing under streetlights — so that parts of daily life now feel contaminated by that scene.

Since then, Priya has found that the workplace itself can set everything off. Her office is in a similar downtown area, and even arriving at the building can tighten her chest: the parking garage, the crosswalk outside, the sight of coworkers stepping into traffic with laptops and coffee cups can pull her back toward the accident. She is especially thrown by reminders of the injured man and by strangers who resemble him in age, build, or dress. On days when she notices someone outside the office who looks like him, or catches herself picturing his body on the road, she starts mentally circling the same question: how exactly could she have prevented it? She replays the light, the angle of the turn, whether she should have left work later, braked sooner, looked twice. At the same time, she tries to force the images away, telling herself not to think about it, and she has largely stopped driving at all, refusing even to be a passenger if she can help it. Her husband now does most of the transportation, and she pays for rideshares to avoid sitting in a car with the sense that it could happen again.

Over the following months these habits hardened rather than eased things. The more Priya tried to shut the thoughts down, the more abruptly they seemed to return when she was at work or passing through the parts of the city that resembled the crash site. She can spend a lunch break trying not to picture the victim, only to find that a man in similar clothes entering the elevator brings the image back in full force. Her hours as a UX designer have become more complicated because commuting to the office has become an ordeal; she often negotiates remote days or arrives visibly tense after a rideshare route through downtown. In meetings she can lose the thread when her mind starts calculating alternate timelines in which no one was hurt. She knows this rumination goes nowhere, but she feels compelled by it, as if finding the precise missed moment might somehow make what happened less unbearable.

Avoiding cars has also made the world feel narrower and, in an unexpected way, has left the triggers more potent. Because she no longer drives and rarely rides with others, she has had less chance to discover whether she can tolerate roads, intersections, and pedestrians without catastrophe. Instead, each necessary trip feels exceptional and charged. If a rideshare slows for a crosswalk near her office, she becomes rigid and stares straight ahead, trying to blank her mind; later that same day she may be even more alert to anyone who resembles the injured man. The office has stopped being just a workplace and become one of the places where she braces for reminders. What frightened her most was how quickly an ordinary workday could collapse into mental replay, and she had come to believe that if she let herself think about the accident freely, or got into a car casually, she would either fall apart or prove she had learned nothing.

Priya finally sought help after her husband told her their life was shrinking around the accident. He had begun arranging his own schedule around driving her, and she had turned down an in-person design workshop because it required traveling across the city. She was ashamed of how much of her day was now spent either trying not to think about the injured man or going over, again and again, how she should have prevented his injuries. Sitting in the intake, she said she wanted to be able to go to work without scanning every street corner for someone who looked like him, and to sit in a car without feeling she was stepping back into the worst moment of her life. What she fears most is that this means she is still dangerous; what she hopes, more quietly, is that she might someday move through her own city without every reminder turning her back toward that intersection.
